title: Magnetism
seo_title: Secondary 4 Physics: Magnetism Worksheets (O-Level 6091 with Answers)
standard_text: State the properties of magnets; describe induced magnetism; distinguish between magnetic and non-magnetic materials; describe methods of magnetisation using a direct current in a solenoid and methods of demagnetisation; distinguish between the properties and uses of temporary (soft iron) and permanent (steel) magnets; draw the magnetic field pattern around a bar magnet and between two magnets, and describe the use of plotting compasses (summary of the Singapore-Cambridge O-Level Physics 6091 syllabus).
meta_desc: Free Secondary 4 O-Level Physics worksheets on magnetism: magnetic poles, magnetic materials, induced magnetism, soft iron and steel, magnetisation and magnetic field patterns. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Like poles repel; unlike poles attract.
key_sub: Soft iron: temporary magnets. Steel: permanent magnets.
body_html:
How to think about it

Every magnet has a north pole and a south pole.

  • Like poles repel, unlike poles attract. A magnet attracts magnetic materials (iron, steel, nickel, cobalt) by induced magnetism.
  • Only repulsion proves that an object is a magnet.
  • Soft iron is easily magnetised and demagnetised (temporary magnets, electromagnet cores); steel keeps its magnetism (permanent magnets).
  • Field lines go from N to S outside the magnet and are closest at the poles. A plotting compass shows the field direction.
Example

A bar is attracted by both poles of a magnet. Is it a magnet?

a magnet would repel one pole

Answer: No: it is a magnetic material

Example

Best core for a scrapyard electromagnet?

must lose magnetism when switched off

Answer: soft iron

Common mistakes

  • Thinking all metals are magnetic. Copper, aluminium and brass are not.
  • Using attraction as proof that something is a magnet.
  • Drawing field lines from S to N outside a magnet.
  • Choosing steel for an electromagnet core.

faq.a: Iron, steel, nickel and cobalt, and alloys containing them. Copper, aluminium, brass, gold and plastics are not magnetic.

faq.q: What is the difference between soft iron and steel?
faq.a: Soft iron is magnetised and demagnetised easily, so it makes temporary magnets; steel is harder to magnetise but keeps its magnetism, so it makes permanent magnets.

faq.q: How do you draw the field around a bar magnet?
faq.a: Draw lines leaving the north pole and curving round into the south pole, with arrows from N to S and lines closest together near the poles.

items.q: The S pole of one magnet is brought near the N pole of another. What happens?
items.e: Like poles repel; unlike poles attract.

items.q: What are iron filings used for near a magnet?
c: to measure the strength of the magnet in newtons

items.e: They line up along the field lines.

items.q: A magnet is held near a copper wire, an iron nail, a wooden pencil and a glass marble. Which one is attracted?
items.e: Only iron, steel, nickel and cobalt are attracted to magnets.

items.q: The S pole of a magnet is brought near an unmagnetised iron nail. What happens?
c: The nail is attracted only to the S pole.
items.e: The nail becomes an induced magnet with the opposite pole nearest, so it is attracted to either pole.

items.q: What is a magnetic field?

the path of an electric current

straight lines from one N to the other
items.e: Field lines go from N to S outside a magnet; closer lines mean a stronger field.
